title: How to Love Your Actual Neighbors
excerpt: We talk about loving humanity while not knowing the names of the people on our own street. Jesus made the neighbor specific on purpose.
body:
A lawyer once tried to get Jesus to define the word neighbor so he could limit it. Jesus told him a story about a man bleeding in a ditch and the unlikely stranger who stopped, and then he flipped the question. The lawyer wanted to know who counted as his neighbor. Jesus asked instead who acted like one. The lawyer wanted a boundary. Jesus gave him a verb.

This matters because most of us love an abstraction. We care about humanity, about justice, about the poor in general, while remaining strangers to the family forty feet from our front door. It is easier to love the world than the man whose dog barks all night. The world does not annoy you. The neighbor does.

## Know the names

Love begins with knowledge, and knowledge begins with names. You cannot love people you have reduced to the blue house or the loud truck. So start there. Learn the names of the people on either side of you and across the street. If you have lived somewhere for years and do not know them, that is not a logistics problem. That is a window into how we have built our lives to need no one.

I lived next to a man for three years and knew only that he left early and came home late. When his wife finally told me he had been driving an hour each way to sit with his dying mother, I felt the weight of all the times I had judged his closed garage door for a story I had invented. Knowing the name would have spared me the false story.

## Be available before you are useful

We want to help in big ways at the dramatic moment. But neighbor love is mostly small and unglamorous. It is the package brought to the porch. The trash cans rolled back up the driveway. The wave that becomes a conversation that becomes a sense, over months, that this is a person who notices. Availability is the currency. You have to be around, and you have to be unhurried enough to stop.

This is hard precisely because our schedules are engineered for efficiency, and neighbor love is inefficient. It interrupts. The Samaritan was going somewhere. He let the man in the ditch change his plans. That is the cost, and there is no version without it.

## Accept help, not only give it

We think of loving our neighbors as a one-way gift, and that instinct can be a quiet form of pride. To always be the helper is to always be above. Real neighborliness includes letting them help you. Borrow the ladder. Ask them to watch the house. Receive the casserole when you are sick. Need is the doorway to relationship, and we will not let our neighbors through it because we are ashamed to be seen needing anything. Bell, you do this too. The hardest evangelism is admitting you are not self-sufficient.

## Cross the lines you would rather keep

The shock of the parable is that the one who stopped was a Samaritan, a member of the group the lawyer despised. Jesus did not pick a respectable hero. He picked the outsider. The point lands on us when the neighbor we are called to love votes differently, believes differently, lives in a way we find hard to understand. Loving the neighbor who is just like us is not what Jesus commended. Anyone does that. The love that testifies to something beyond ordinary self-interest is the love that crosses the line we drew.

## Let love be slow

None of this converts on a timeline. You may love your neighbors for years before any conversation about faith ever happens, and it may never happen the way you hoped. That is not failure. You are not loving them in order to close a sale. You are loving them because they bear the image of God and live near you, and that is reason enough. If a deeper conversation comes, it will come out of trust that took years to build, and it will be real because the love was real first.

## This week

Walk outside and learn one name you do not know. Then do one small, unrequested thing for that household: the cans, the package, a plate of something. Do not announce it. Do not attach a tract. Just be the kind of presence that, over time, makes a person think this neighborhood holds someone who sees them. Loving your actual neighbors starts with the word actual, and the word actual means the ones who are really there, not the ones you imagine you would love if they were easier.
